solution:
Let \(\vec{m}=xc\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}\), \(\vec{n}=x\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2cx\hat{k}\).
\(\vec{m}\cdot\vec{n}=cx^2-12+6cx=cx^2+6cx-12\)
For an obtuse angle we need \(\vec{m}\cdot\vec{n}<0\) for every real \(x\).
For \(c \neq 0\), treating \(f(x)=cx^2+6cx-12\) as a quadratic in \(x\), for \(f(x)<0\) for all \(x\) we need \(c<0\) (downward-opening parabola) and discriminant \(<0\):
\((6c)^2-4c(-12)<0\ \Rightarrow\ 36c^2+48c<0\ \Rightarrow\ 12c(3c+4)<0\ \Rightarrow\ -\dfrac43<c<0\)
If \(c=0\), \(f(x)=-12<0\) for every \(x\), and \(-6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}\) and \(x\hat{i}+2\hat{j}\) are never parallel, so \(c=0\) works too.
Hence \(-\dfrac43<c\le 0\).
note: c = 0 was missed: then m.n = -12 < 0 for every x and the vectors are never parallel, so the answer is -4/3 < c <= 0.

solution: Let A, B and C be the vertices of a triangle. Let AD, BE and CF be the altitudes of the triangle ABC, therefore \(AD \perp BC\), \(BE \perp AC\), \(CF \perp AB\). Let \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}, \vec{d}, \vec{e}, \vec{f}\) be the position vectors of A, B, C, D, E, F respectively. Let P be the point of intersection of the altitudes AD and BE with \(\vec{p}\) as the position vector. Therefore, \(\vec{AP}\perp\vec{BC}, \vec{BP}\perp\vec{AC}\) .......(1). To show that the altitudes AD, BE and CF are concurrent, it is sufficient to show that the altitude CF passes through the point P. We will have to prove that \(\vec{CF}\) and \(\vec{CP}\) are collinear vectors. This can be achieved by showing \(\vec{CP}\perp\vec{AB}\). Now from (1) we have \(\vec{AP}\perp\vec{BC}\) and \(\vec{BP}\perp\vec{AC}\). \(\therefore \vec{AP}\cdot\vec{BC} = 0\) and \(\vec{BP}\cdot\vec{AC} = 0\). \(\therefore (\vec{p}-\vec{a})\cdot(\vec{c}-\vec{b}) = 0\) and \((\vec{p}-\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{c}-\vec{a}) = 0\). \(\therefore \vec{p}\cdot\vec{c}-\vec{p}\cdot\vec{b}-\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}+\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\) .....(2). \(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{c}-\vec{p}\cdot\vec{a}-\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}+\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a} = 0\) ......(3). Therefore, subtracting equation (2) from equation (3), we get \(-\vec{p}\cdot\vec{a}+\vec{p}\cdot\vec{b}-\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}+\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} = 0\) (Since \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}\)). \(\therefore \vec{p}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{a})-\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{a}) = 0\). \(\therefore (\vec{p}-\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{a}) = 0\). \(\therefore \vec{CP}\cdot\vec{AB} = 0\). \(\therefore \vec{CP}\perp\vec{AB}\). Hence the proof.

**Part 1: the theorem.**

Let \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\) be non-collinear (so both are non-zero and neither is a scalar multiple of the other), and let \(\overrightarrow{r}\) be coplanar with them.

*Existence.* Take a point \(O\) as origin and let \(\overrightarrow{OA} = \overrightarrow{a}\), \(\overrightarrow{OB} = \overrightarrow{b}\), \(\overrightarrow{OR} = \overrightarrow{r}\). Since \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\) are non-collinear, the points \(O\), \(A\), \(B\) are not collinear and so determine a unique plane; as \(\overrightarrow{r}\) is coplanar with \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\), the point \(R\) lies in that same plane.

Through \(R\) draw a line parallel to \(OB\), meeting line \(OA\) at \(P\), and a line parallel to \(OA\), meeting line \(OB\) at \(Q\). Then \(OPRQ\) is a parallelogram, so by the triangle law
\(\overrightarrow{OR} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PR} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{OQ}\)

Now \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) lies along the line \(OA\), so \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) is a scalar multiple of \(\overrightarrow{a}\): \(\overrightarrow{OP} = t_{1}\overrightarrow{a}\) for some scalar \(t_{1}\). Similarly \(\overrightarrow{OQ} = t_{2}\overrightarrow{b}\).

\(\therefore \overrightarrow{r} = t_{1}\overrightarrow{a} + t_{2}\overrightarrow{b}\)

*Uniqueness.* Suppose also \(\overrightarrow{r} = s_{1}\overrightarrow{a} + s_{2}\overrightarrow{b}\). Subtracting,
\(\left( t_{1} - s_{1} \right)\overrightarrow{a} + \left( t_{2} - s_{2} \right)\overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{0}\)

If \(t_{1} - s_{1} \neq 0\), then
\(\overrightarrow{a} = -\dfrac{t_{2} - s_{2}}{t_{1} - s_{1}}\,\overrightarrow{b}\),
making \(\overrightarrow{a}\) a scalar multiple of \(\overrightarrow{b}\), i.e. \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\) collinear, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence \(t_{1} = s_{1}\).

Then \(\left( t_{2} - s_{2} \right)\overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{0}\) with \(\overrightarrow{b} \neq \overrightarrow{0}\), so \(t_{2} = s_{2}\).

The scalars \(t_{1}\) and \(t_{2}\) are therefore unique.

**Part 2: the computation.**

\(\overrightarrow{r} = t_{1}\overrightarrow{a} + t_{2}\overrightarrow{b}\)
\(\therefore 2\widehat{i} + 7\widehat{j} + 9\widehat{k} = t_{1}\left( \widehat{i} + 2\widehat{j} \right) + t_{2}\left( \widehat{j} + 3\widehat{k} \right)\)
\(\therefore 2\widehat{i} + 7\widehat{j} + 9\widehat{k} = t_{1}\widehat{i} + \left( 2t_{1} + t_{2} \right)\widehat{j} + 3t_{2}\widehat{k}\)

By equality of two vectors,
\(t_{1} = 2\) ... (1)
\(2t_{1} + t_{2} = 7\) ... (2)
\(3t_{2} = 9\) ... (3)

From (3), \(t_{2} = 3\). Equation (2) is then satisfied: \(2(2) + 3 = 7\). (Consistency of equation (2), the one not used to find \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), is what confirms that \(\overrightarrow{r}\) really is coplanar with \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\).)

**Answer:** \(t_{1} = 2\), \(t_{2} = 3\)
note: t1 comes from (1) and t2 from (3); the equation checked is (2), not the third.

solution:
Let \(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d\) be position vectors of A, B, C, D.
\(\overline{AB}\times\overline{CD}=(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec d-\vec c)=\vec b\times\vec d-\vec b\times\vec c-\vec a\times\vec d+\vec a\times\vec c\)
\(\overline{BC}\times\overline{AD}=(\vec c-\vec b)\times(\vec d-\vec a)=\vec c\times\vec d-\vec c\times\vec a-\vec b\times\vec d+\vec b\times\vec a\)
\(\overline{CA}\times\overline{BD}=(\vec a-\vec c)\times(\vec d-\vec b)=\vec a\times\vec d-\vec a\times\vec b-\vec c\times\vec d+\vec c\times\vec b\)
Adding all three, the \(\vec b\times\vec d\), \(\vec c\times\vec d\), and \(\vec a\times\vec d\) terms cancel in pairs, leaving
Sum \(=-2(\vec b\times\vec c)+2(\vec a\times\vec c)-2(\vec a\times\vec b)=-2(\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a)\).
By the standard result, Area\((\triangle ABC)=\dfrac12|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a|\), i.e. \(|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a|=2\,\text{area}(\triangle ABC)\).
Hence \(|\overline{AB}\times\overline{CD}+\overline{BC}\times\overline{AD}+\overline{CA}\times\overline{BD}|=2\times2\,\text{area}(\triangle ABC)=\mathbf{4\,\text{area}(\triangle ABC)}\). Hence proved.

solution:
Given \(\vec{c}=3\vec{a}-2\vec{b}\).
By linearity of the scalar triple product in the third slot:
\([\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a}\ \ \vec{b}\ \ 3\vec{a}-2\vec{b}] = 3[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{a}] - 2[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{b}]\)
Both \([\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{a}]\) and \([\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{b}]\) are \(0\), since each has a repeated vector.
\(\therefore [\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}] = 3(0) - 2(0) = \mathbf{0}\). Hence proved.
(This is consistent with the given condition \([\vec{a}\ \ \vec{b}+\vec{c}\ \ \vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}]=0\), which in fact holds identically for any \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\).)

solution:
Take the circumcenter Q as the origin, with \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\) the position vectors of A, B, C (\(|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=R\)). The orthocenter P then has position vector
\(\overrightarrow{QP}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\)
(verified by checking \(AH\perp BC\), \(BH\perp CA\), \(CH\perp AB\) for the point H with this position vector).
The centroid G of \(\triangle ABC\) has position vector
\(\overrightarrow{QG}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{3}\)
Therefore,
\(3\overrightarrow{QG}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\overrightarrow{QP}\)
**Hence \(\overrightarrow{QP}=3\overrightarrow{QG}\), as required.** (This also shows Q, G, P are collinear: the Euler line of the triangle.)

solution:
From \(\vec a\times\vec b=\vec a\times\vec c\): \(\vec a\times(\vec b-\vec c)=\vec 0\Rightarrow\vec b-\vec c=\lambda\vec a\) for some scalar \(\lambda\) (since \(\vec a\ne\vec 0\)).
From \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec c\): \(\vec a\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0\). Substituting \(\vec b-\vec c=\lambda\vec a\):
\(\vec a\cdot(\lambda\vec a)=\lambda|\vec a|^2=0\).
Since \(\vec a\ne\vec 0\), \(|\vec a|^2\ne0\), so \(\lambda=0\), giving \(\vec b-\vec c=\vec 0\), i.e. \(\mathbf{\vec b=\vec c}\). \(\mathbf{Answer: Yes}\).
